questions.stem: Why is a thin leaf an advantage for diffusion?

options.text: It shortens the diffusion distance into the cells
options.explanation: Less distance means faster exchange.
Flatness gives area; thinness gives a short path.
Thinness does not block anything; it speeds entry.
Strength is not the exchange reason.
They dot the surfaces, not the margins.
The lower surface carries most of the pores.
The upper surface usually has few or none.
Stomata are epidermal pores, not internal gaps.

questions.stem: What fills the gaps between spongy mesophyll cells?

options.explanation: Chloroplasts sit inside cells, not between them.
Xylem runs in veins, not between mesophyll cells.
The loose packing leaves room for gas circulation.
The spaces are air-filled; moisture films coat the cells.

questions.stem: Which route does carbon dioxide take into a photosynthesising cell?

options.explanation: Xylem carries water, not gases.
Phloem carries sugars, not gas entry.
That is water's route, not carbon dioxide's direct gas path.

options.text: Atmosphere, air spaces, mesophyll cells, chloroplast
options.explanation: That is the named diffusion pathway.

questions.stem: Why do the cell walls' thinness matter for gas exchange?

options.text: Gases pass easily through thin walls into the cells
options.explanation: Every layer's thinness shortens the total journey.
Walls do not store anything.
Light matters for photosynthesis but not for wall thinness here.
If anything, easy gas passage trades off against water retention.

questions.stem: Name the three gases involved in leaf exchange.
questions.modelAnswer: Carbon dioxide, oxygen and water vapour.

questions.stem: Give two whole-leaf adaptations for gas exchange.
questions.modelAnswer: Thin, for a short diffusion distance, and broad or flat, for a large surface area, with many stomata for entry.

questions.stem: Explain why the air spaces are an internal adaptation.
questions.modelAnswer: Because they let gases circulate around the loosely packed mesophyll cells, so every cell touches an air pocket and the exchange surface reaches deep inside the leaf rather than stopping at the epidermis.

questions.stem: A botanist compares a thick succulent leaf with a thin mesophyte leaf. Predict the exchange rates and justify with the adaptations.
questions.modelAnswer: The thin leaf exchanges faster: its shorter diffusion distance and loosely packed air spaces give gases quicker access to every cell, while the succulent's bulky, water-storing interior lengthens the path and trades exchange speed for drought survival.

options.text: A broken hair on the leaf
options.explanation: Leaf hairs are separate structures.

options.text: A gap between two guard cells
options.explanation: The pore exists where the pair of guard cells parts.
Nothing burns; the pore is built from cells.

options.text: A split in the waxy cuticle
options.explanation: The cuticle covers the surfaces; the pore is cellular.

questions.stem: What makes guard cells open the pore?

options.explanation: No air pressure is involved.
Nothing melts; osmosis does the work.

options.text: Water entering them by osmosis makes them turgid
options.explanation: Swelling bends the pair apart and opens the gap.
Losing water closes the pore.

questions.stem: When do stomata tend to close?

options.text: When water is plentiful and light is strong
options.explanation: Those favour opening.
Fast photosynthesis needs open pores for carbon dioxide.
The valve action opens and closes them constantly.

options.text: When water is scarce or sunlight is low
options.explanation: Both conditions favour the flaccid, closed state.

questions.stem: What is the cost of open stomata?

options.text: Water vapour escapes while gases enter
options.explanation: The open pore serves exchange and leaks at the same time.

options.text: Carbon dioxide cannot enter while open
options.explanation: Entry is exactly what openness provides.

options.text: The leaf loses its green colour
options.explanation: Colour is untouched by pore state.
Open pores feed photosynthesis; they do not stop it.

questions.stem: Why does closing stomata protect a plant in drought?

options.text: It lowers the leaf's temperature only
options.explanation: Temperature effects are secondary; the protection is water retention.

options.text: It blocks water vapour from escaping through the pores
options.explanation: Sealing the valves holds the leaf's water in.

options.text: It stops sunlight damaging the cells
options.explanation: Closing is about water, not light.

options.text: It keeps carbon dioxide inside for later
options.explanation: Nothing is stored for later; closing halts exchange.

questions.modelAnswer: A pore between two guard cells, mostly on the lower epidermis, through which gases diffuse.

questions.stem: State the two states of a guard cell pair and what each does to the pore.
questions.modelAnswer: Turgid guard cells open the pore; flaccid guard cells close it.

questions.stem: Explain why stomata sit mostly on the lower epidermis.
questions.modelAnswer: Because the underside is shaded and cooler, so open pores there lose less water vapour than they would on the sunnier top surface; the placement limits the leak while keeping exchange available.

questions.stem: Midday drought hits a sunlit leaf. Describe the guard cells' response and its consequence for the leaf's day.
questions.modelAnswer: Water drains from the guard cells by osmosis, they turn flaccid, and the pores close; carbon dioxide entry stops so photosynthesis slows, oxygen exit and vapour loss also stop, and the leaf rides out the drought on stored resources.
